speaker: Soumith Chintala
title: The Gradient Podcast - Soumith Chintala: PyTorch
question: When adding a compiler stack to an eager-mode machine learning framework, why use partial-graph compilation instead of requiring whole-program compilation?
guest: Remember how we bet on modelers and modeling being pretty important? One of the central effects of that thesis is eager mode, which means when you're doing modeling, you iterate on your program without any constraints. You can write for loops, ifs, whiles—anything you want—and that's our problem. With PyTorch 2.0, one of the central things we absolutely wanted to nail was to keep that alive, that it's our problem how to compile the program. If we can't compile it or part of it, we shouldn't, and you shouldn't be thinking or caring about it. So we built 2.0 entirely around partial graphs, where we trace the program, the parts that we can compile we will, and the parts that we can't compile we just leave alone. That is what compiler writers actually hate, and that goes back to the trade-offs. We explicitly said, 'Yeah, it's going to be harder to write the compiler, but we're not optimizing for compiler people to have an easy life—we're optimizing for modelers to have an easy life.'

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Partial-graph compilation exists because real eager-mode programs are ordinary Python, and ordinary Python is rarely compilable in full. User code freely mixes tensor operations with data-dependent control flow, dynamic shapes, side effects like printing and logging, calls into NumPy or other third-party libraries, and arbitrary language features. A whole-program compiler (such as TorchScript's scripting mode) must either support all of this or reject the program, which forces users to rewrite models into a restricted language subset and gives up the flexibility and debuggability that made eager mode attractive in the first place.

Partial-graph compilation, as in PyTorch 2's TorchDynamo, sidesteps this. The compiler captures the regions it can understand as graphs, optimizes them, and when it hits something unsupported it inserts a "graph break," falls back to the normal Python interpreter for that piece, then resumes capturing afterward. Guards check that the assumptions behind each compiled region still hold, triggering recompilation otherwise.

The result is that compilation is opt-in and incremental: nearly all existing code runs unmodified and correctly, the compilable parts get the speedups, and the cost is only lost cross-region optimization, not a broken program.

models.label: Gemini 4 Carbon
models.answer:
Eager-mode machine learning frameworks owe their popularity to full host-language flexibility: users freely interleave tensor operations with arbitrary Python control flow, dynamic shapes, custom data structures, third-party C/C++ libraries, and interactive debugging. Requiring whole-program compilation forces the entire execution into a single static graph, which fails outright or demands costly rewrites into a restricted language subset whenever it encounters unsupported constructs, side effects, or data-dependent branching—a major adoption barrier seen in earlier systems like TorchScript.

Partial-graph compilation resolves this tension between ergonomics and performance through graceful degradation. Rather than rejecting untraceable code, the compiler captures and optimizes maximal supported tensor subgraphs—enabling kernel fusion and memory planning—while inserting graph breaks that fall back to the eager interpreter for unsupported host operations before resuming compilation. This preserves exact eager semantics, interactive debugging, and out-of-the-box compatibility with unmodified codebases, while still capturing most of the available speedup by accelerating the compute-dense regions that dominate execution time.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
Partial-graph compilation keeps the framework's main strength, which is that arbitrary Python just works, while still getting most of the speedups a compiler can give. PyTorch 2's TorchDynamo is the standard example.

Eager-mode users write unrestricted Python: data-dependent control flow, third-party libraries, printing, logging, NumPy calls, custom objects, and dynamic shapes. Whole-program approaches like TorchScript, symbolic tracing, or `tf.function`-style tracing require all of that to fit a restricted, capturable subset. In practice that means rewriting models, silent wrong results when tracing misses a branch, or outright failures. Those costs pushed users away from earlier graph modes.

With partial-graph capture, the system works at the bytecode level. It extracts the tensor-heavy regions it understands into graphs and hands those to a backend such as Inductor. When it hits something it can't handle, it falls back to normal Python, which is called a "graph break," and resumes capture afterward. Guards check the assumptions each compiled graph relies on and recompile when they fail.

The result is that compilation is opt-in and incremental, so a one-line `torch.compile` works on almost any model. Correctness is never worse than eager, and since most runtime sits in a few large tensor regions, you still get most of the performance.

models.label: Gemini 4 Neon
models.answer:
Requiring whole-program compilation in an eager-mode machine learning framework is brittle because real-world models rely heavily on dynamic host-language features—such as data-dependent control flow, arbitrary third-party libraries, logging, custom extensions, and dynamic shapes—that static compiler frontends cannot always capture or lower. When a whole-program compiler encounters any unsupported construct, compilation fails outright, forcing developers to rewrite models into a restricted subset of the language and sacrificing the flexibility and debuggability that made eager execution appealing in the first place.

Partial-graph compilation avoids this all-or-nothing trade-off by compiling the tensor-heavy subgraphs it understands and inserting graph breaks to fall back gracefully to the eager runtime for unsupported regions. This preserves full language compatibility and lets existing codebases adopt compilation incrementally with minimal modification. Because most compute time is concentrated in standard tensor operations anyway, partial-graph compilation still captures the bulk of optimization benefits—like operator fusion, memory planning, and kernel code generation—while keeping compilation times, debugging, and maintenance far more manageable.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
Partial-graph compilation lets an eager-mode framework speed up the parts of a program it can compile while preserving normal execution everywhere else. Real models often mix tensor operations with data-dependent Python control flow, I/O, debugging code, or custom operations the compiler cannot trace. With partial graphs, the compiler can optimize a region of tensor operations, fall back to eager execution at an unsupported operation, and resume compilation afterward. If whole-program compilation is required, a single unsupported operation can prevent the entire program from compiling or force the user to rewrite it.

The tradeoff is that graph boundaries add overhead and limit optimizations such as operator fusion across those boundaries. In practice, compiling the regions where most computation happens can capture much of the speedup while letting users keep their existing code and adopt compilation incrementally.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Astra
models.answer:
Partial-graph compilation lets users keep writing eager-mode code while the compiler optimizes the parts it understands. A model may mix long stretches of tensor operations with data-dependent Python control flow, side effects, or calls to external libraries. If the compiler requires a single graph, one unsupported operation can force the user to rewrite the code or give up compilation for the entire program.

With partial-graph compilation, the framework can compile the tensor operations before a graph break, run the unsupported code eagerly, and resume compilation afterward. This preserves eager behavior and can speed up the computationally expensive parts without requiring a rewrite. The trade-off is that graph breaks add overhead and can prevent optimizations, such as fusing operations across the break.
